claims.text: Surface segregation in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles reduces surface cohesive energy.
Reduced surface cohesive energy lowers the onset temperatures of premelting and melting relative to nanoparticles with homogeneous surface composition.
The initial high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles have homogeneous elemental mixing.
A controlled thermal pretreatment can promote surface segregation without changing the overall bulk composition.
The controlled comparison uses a segregated, pretreated group and an untreated, compositionally homogeneous group.
Both groups are heated at 5 K/min in an inert atmosphere and monitored by in-situ TEM and DSC.
Surface enrichment of selected alloying elements mediates changes in surface cohesive energy.
Segregation creates localized surface regions with reduced cohesive energy.
Surface regions with reduced cohesive energy initiate surface premelting earlier.
Earlier surface premelting leads to a lower overall melting temperature.
Segregated nanoparticles will exhibit lower onset temperatures for both premelting and melting than the homogeneous baseline.
DSC will show a lower-temperature melting endotherm for segregated nanoparticles.
In-situ TEM will reveal earlier surface melting in segregated nanoparticles.
High-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are relevant to catalysis, chemical sensing, and energy applications.
The proposed segregation effect should hold across nanoparticle sizes and compositions typical of catalysis, sensing, and energy applications under inert, controlled heating.
The effect may fail for sufficiently large particles.
The effect may fail when pretreatment causes substantial morphological changes beyond surface segregation.
EDS mapping during heating can verify the presence and extent of surface segregation.
Failure to observe a statistically significant decrease in premelting or melting onset, or observation of an increase, would falsify the hypothesis.
